name: Lukasova lipa (the Singing Linden of Teleci)

location.address: Beside house no. 102, Teleci, Svitavy District, Pardubice Region
location.neighbourhood: Teleci village, Zdarske vrchy protected landscape area

access: Free. Stands in the open village of Teleci beside house no. 102, about 100 m from the main road; a public pilgrimage tree (Tree of the Year 2021 national winner), not fenced off.
transport: No public transport within 30 min; nearest town Policka is about 8 km away. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
A scribe named Jirousek is said to have hidden inside this trunk in the late 17th century, copying religious books the Counter-Reformation had banned, working by candlelight. Villagers who passed at night heard something coming out of the tree and said it was singing. That part is local tradition rather than record, but the hollow it turns on is real: the trunk is open at ground level and a person fits inside it.

Both sources that describe the tree give an age of 600 to 700 years, and neither shows how the figure was reached, so treat it as the received one rather than a measurement. The girth is measured. Somebody taped it at 962 centimetres in 1899 and it is around 1,170 now, which puts it among the largest limes in eastern Bohemia. The crown reaches 21 to 23 metres depending on which survey year you read.

It has been a protected cultural monument since 1978 and a national heritage tree since 1995. Teleci put it on the village coat of arms and the post office put it on a stamp. In 2021 the country voted it Czech Tree of the Year.

It stands beside house number 102, about a hundred metres off the main road, unfenced, with the hollow trunk given maintenance work every couple of years to keep it upright.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the whole open village smells of it

name: Pernstejnsky tis (the Pernstejn Yew)

location.address: Forest park below Pernstejn Castle, near the path from Nedvedice to the castle courtyard
location.neighbourhood: Nedvedice, Zdar nad Sazavou District, Vysocina Region

access: Free to view. Stands beside the public walking path leading from Nedvedice up to Pernstejn Castle, on the north slope in the castle forest park; reachable on foot without a castle admission ticket. One source describes it more generally as "on castle grounds" so treat as approximate rather than guaranteed unticketed access.
transport: Nedvedice railway station is about 1.5-2 km / 20-25 min walk. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
Local belief holds that Pernstejn Castle prospers for as long as this yew does. In April 2005 one of its branches broke; on 15 April the castle caught fire. Sources record the coincidence and nobody claims a link, which is about the right amount of weight to give it.

The tree is the oldest yew in Moravia and nobody can tell you how old that is. Popular coverage settles on roughly 1,000 years. The Czech Wikipedia entry collects the estimates that actually exist, and they run from 400 years to 2,000, with the folklore figures clustering between 760 and 1,050. Take the round thousand as the number people repeat rather than the number anyone has established. What has been measured is the trunk: about 410 centimetres round in 1900, about 450 today, standing 15 to 16.5 metres.

The founding story is that a pilgrim pushed his yew walking staff into the ground here and it rooted. The country voted it Czech Tree of the Year in 2005. A survey in 2001 put its vitality at three out of five, ageing but alive.

It stands on the north slope of the castle forest park, beside the walking path up from Nedvedice, and can be reached on foot without a castle ticket, though one description places it more loosely on the castle grounds.

name: Popovsky jasan (the Popov Ash)

location.address: Site of the vanished village of Popov, northwest of the Popov cross, near Jachymov
location.neighbourhood: Popov (defunct settlement), Jachymov, Karlovy Vary District, Krusne Mountains

access: Free. Reached on foot via a marked green tourist trail from Jachymov town hall/St Anna chapel, through forest paths climbing toward Marianska; the tree stands in open ground at the site of the vanished village, no gate or ticket.
transport: No public transport to the site itself; Jachymov town (with rail/bus links) is the trailhead, roughly 3-4 km / 45-60 min walk uphill. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
The village this ash grew up in is gone. Popov was a German-speaking settlement in the Krusne Mountains until its people were expelled after the Second World War and the houses came down. The tree is still standing in the middle of it, roots spread over the stone foundations of one of them, which is the closest thing to a street plan the site has left.

It is one of the largest ash trees in the country. Somebody measured 682 centimetres round with a 24 metre crown spread in 2004, and 737 more recently, so it is still putting on wood at over thirty metres tall. Sources give the age as about 200 years and none of them shows the working, so read it as the received figure.

It spent decades unvisited and was found again in the early 1990s by a dentist from Karlovy Vary. Protection followed in 2003, and in 2002 more than 1,300 voters made it Czech Tree of the Year. Nobody has published a health assessment since 2004; the town's own walking guide says as much.

Getting there is the walk. A green trail leaves Jachymov by the St Anne chapel and climbs through forest toward Marianska, three or four kilometres of uphill, and the tree stands in open ground where the village used to be.

name: Lipa v Lipce (the Linden of Lipka)

location.address: Beside the path to the Kustos family tomb, near the former Gothic fortress, Lipka
location.neighbourhood: Lipka, Horni Bradlo, Chrudim District, Zelezne hory Protected Landscape Area

access: Free. Stands beside a yellow-marked hiking trail/path leading to the Kustos family tomb near a former Gothic fortress; open countryside, no gate or ticket.
transport: No public transport to the site itself; Horni Bradlo village is about 1 km away. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
This lime lost a third of itself and came back looking deliberate. It grew on three trunks, one of them broke away, and the wound closed into the balanced twin-stemmed shape it carries now, with a hollow running from the base up into the crown. That crown is 26 metres across, on a tree standing somewhere between 27 and 32 metres tall.

The trunk measured 802 centimetres round when it was first taped, 870 in 2001 and 905 in 2016, which ranks it among the five biggest small-leaved limes in Bohemia by girth. Its age is given as 600 to 800 years, a band nobody has narrowed, and the tree is more convincing than the number.

In 2016 the Czech public voted it Tree of the Year, and it went on to take third place in the European Tree of the Year in 2017, which is a lot of votes for a tree standing on a field path in the Zelezne hory. It has been protected since 1990. Cables were fitted in the crown to hold the stems, in place as of 2020, and it is described as in good health for its age.

It stands beside the yellow-marked path that runs to the Kustos family tomb, near the site of a former Gothic fortress. No gate, no ticket.

best_time.label: late June into July, when a crown twenty-six metres across comes into flower

name: Tatobitska lipa (the Thousand-Year Lime of Tatobity)
age_estimate: 500 to 1,000 years (locally nicknamed the thousand-year lime)

location.address: Near house no. 86, beside the road toward Zernov, Tatobity
location.neighbourhood: Tatobity, Semily District, Liberec Region, on the edge of the Cesky raj (Bohemian Paradise)

access: Free. Stands beside the road toward Zernov in the open village of Tatobity, near residential houses; no gate or ticket.
transport: No public transport to the village itself within 30 min; nearest town Semily is about 8 km away. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
Ten people fit inside the trunk, which is hollow from the ground up and has been held together by two iron bands since the 1920s. A local youth association fenced and reinforced the tree in 1923; the bands are still doing the work.

The village calls it the thousand-year lime, and the sources will not back that up. Czech Wikipedia gives 500 to 800 years. The Tree of the Year foundation gives 600 to 1,000, with an 800-year estimate drawn from measurements taken in 2009. Nobody has resolved the gap, so the honest answer is somewhere between five hundred and a thousand and the nickname is a nickname. The measured part is steadier: 866 centimetres round in 1993, 940 in 1996, 956 in 2009, on a tree 17 to 20 metres tall. It was given remedial treatment in 1995 and has been protected since 1979.

What it is genuinely famous for is a vote. In 2015 the country made it Czech Tree of the Year, and in 2016 it came second in the European Tree of the Year with more than 43,000 votes behind it. That is the most recent dated report of the tree we found, so if you go and it has changed, tell us.

It stands on the road toward Zernov, among the houses, at the edge of Bohemian Paradise.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the hollow trunk and its iron bands are fully in view

name: Kotelske lipy (the Kotel Lindens)
age_estimate: roughly 950 years for the elder tree (estimates range widely, 350 to 1,100 years)

location.address: Field path at the northeastern edge of the hamlet of Kotel, Osecna
location.neighbourhood: Kotel, Osecna, Liberec District, Podjestedi region

access: Free. Stands on a field path at the edge of Kotel hamlet, reachable via marked blue and yellow hiking trails; open countryside, no restriction found.
transport: No public transport to the hamlet itself; Osecna is about 3 km away. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
When a uranium mine was proposed under the Podjestedi countryside, the campaign against it took these two limes as its emblem. In 2009 the country voted them Czech Tree of the Year, which is one way for a hamlet of a few houses to be heard.

There are two trees standing a few metres apart on the field path at the edge of Kotel, and you look at them as one thing. The elder carries the local name Thousand-Year Lime: 970 centimetres round, 25 metres tall, its trunk split into three hollow stems that a single thick adventitious root has grown down through the middle to prop up. Its neighbour is the younger by some distance at 500 to 600 centimetres round and 23 metres tall.

The headline age of about 950 years is the one repeated everywhere. The estimates that have actually been published run from 350 years to 1,100, and nothing narrows them, so the name is a claim rather than a count. Local tradition has the elder tree standing through a Hussite raid on the village in 1444 and the peasant unrest of 1680; that is village memory, not record.

They have been protected since 1993, and safety work was carried out on the hollow stems around 2015. Blue and yellow trails reach them, over open ground with nothing to pay.

best_time.label: late June into July, when both crowns flower at once and the field path fills with bees

name: Buk v Msseckych Zehrovicich (the Zehrovice Beech)

location.address: North of the village, below the road, near a double bend (severne od obce pod silnici u dvojite zatacky)
location.neighbourhood: Msecke Zehrovice, Rakovnik District, Central Bohemia

access: Free. Stands beside the road on the north edge of the village, near a double bend; publicly visible from the roadside, no restriction.
transport: No public transport to the exact spot; Msecke Zehrovice is served by regional bus, tree is a short walk from the village. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
This beech is dying, and the village has decided not to fight it. A wood-decay fungus is working through the trunk, there is no cure, and the municipality's position as of February 2025 is non-intervention: the tree stays where it is, its death is treated as inevitable, and what is left will stand as deadwood habitat. It was still standing when that notice was written. A sapling cloned from it is already growing a few metres away.

It was called the most beautiful beech in the country once, and the shape that earned it is mostly gone. The crown used to spread around 35 metres. Hurricane Herwart took much of it on 29 October 2017, and photographs from May 2020 show only half of what remains coming into leaf. The trunk is 526 centimetres round, the tree about 21 metres tall. Sources put its age between 350 and 450 years and do not agree with each other; the fungus is named differently by different sources too.

So this is not a visit to a tree at its peak. It is a visit to a large old beech in its last years, standing below the road at the double bend north of the village, with its own replacement rooted beside it. Our pin marks the bend rather than the trunk, so expect to look.

name: Hromuv dub (Hromuv Oak)

location.address: Beside a field track between Hlusovice and Chomoutov, south of Bohunovice
location.neighbourhood: Bohunovice cadastral area, Olomouc District, Olomouc Region

access: Free, reached on foot or by bike along an unmarked dusty field track between the villages of Hlusovice and Chomoutov; no formal tourist trail. One source describes the surrounding ground loosely as private agricultural land, but no gate, fence or restriction on the tree itself was found; flagging rather than blocking.
transport: No public transport to the exact spot; Bohunovice/Chomoutov area is on regional bus routes, tree is a field-track walk from the nearest stop. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
Two information boards stand beside this oak and they disagree with each other. One says the tree is 300 years old, the other says 438. Nobody has settled it, and the Czech Wikipedia entry records the discrepancy rather than choosing, which is the honest position: somewhere between three hundred and four hundred and fifty years, with the boards themselves as the evidence of how loosely that is known.

What the oak is agreed to be is a survivor. It is described as the last of the oaks planted to hold the embankments of the Velky rybnik, the Great Fishpond founded in 1577, and it stands near where the Strazna bouda, the guard cottage, used to be. The cottage is gone and so is the rest of the planting. The tree is 630 centimetres round, up from 600 when it was measured in 2004, and 27 metres tall.

It has been protected since 2005 and had tree surgery in March 2011. In 2010 it won Czech Tree of the Year and went on to represent the country in the European competition.

Getting to it is deliberately unglamorous. A dusty field track runs between Hlusovice and Chomoutov, unmarked and unsignposted, walkable or better on a bike, and the oak is simply standing beside it in the fields. There is no gate and nothing to pay.

name: Lipa Jana Gurreho (the Linden of Jan Gurre)

location.address: By the Church of the Holy Spirit (Kostel svateho Ducha), Rimov village centre
location.neighbourhood: Rimov, Cesky Krumlov District, South Bohemia

access: Free. Stands beside the Church of the Holy Spirit in the centre of the Rimov pilgrimage complex, in the open village; no gate or ticket.
transport: Rimov is served by regional bus from Cesky Budejovice; the tree is a short walk from the stop. NOTE: this candidate is meant to JOIN the existing published Cesky Krumlov city file (per brief, roughly 10km from Zlata Koruna cluster) rather than become its own place.
story:
A pilgrimage site exists because of this tree. In 1626 the Jesuit apothecary Jan Gurre is said to have had a vision beneath it, and to have proposed a Loreto chapel and the Church of the Holy Spirit on the spot partly so that the lime itself would be preserved. What grew out of that is the Rimov complex, big enough that South Bohemians came to call it the European Jerusalem, and the lime is still standing beside the church at the centre of it.

The trunk is completely hollow and kept going by an adventitious root running down through the middle of it. On 15 September 1996, fifty-one people got inside at once and someone counted. It is 760 centimetres round, measured in 2008.

Age is unresolved. The national conservation agency recorded 600 years in 1999 and 650 to 660 in 2008, while other experts on the same record put it nearer 400. The crown is going: 19 metres tall in 1981, roughly 12 to 15 now, as the old limbs die back and the tree lives off stump sprouts.

It was protected in 2000 and took nearly half the national vote as Czech Tree of the Year in 2008. Look for it by the Church of the Holy Spirit; our pin is placed from the address rather than surveyed.

name: Opatovicka borovice (the Opatovice Pine, the Six-Headed Dragon)

location.neighbourhood: Velke Opatovice, Blansko District, South Moravian Region

access: Free. Stands in the Velke Opatovice chateau park, which has been freely open to the public since the early 19th century (13.5 ha, no ticket for the park itself, confirmed by a third source, vikendotevrenychzahrad.cz).
transport: Velke Opatovice has a rail station; the chateau park is a short walk from the centre. Own place, not a city day-trip.
story:
Locally this pine is the six-headed dragon, and the count is literal. The trunk divides into five stems just above the ground, and one of those splits again into three about eight metres up, so the crown reads as a cluster of separate trees that happen to share a base.

That habit also makes its girth an argument. Measured around the whole base cluster it comes to 480 centimetres; measured on the single strongest stem at chest height it is 337. Both numbers are correct and they describe different things. Height is about 20 to 21 metres, and the age is given consistently as around 250 years, which would make it the oldest Austrian pine in the Czech Republic.

It has never been designated a heritage tree in its own right, for the good reason that the whole chateau park around it already carries that protection. The park is 13.5 hectares and has been open to the public since the early 19th century, so the tree has spent its adult life being walked past. It is ageing, described as still vital, and carries dynamic bracing in the crown to hold the stems against wind.

In 2014 the country voted it Czech Tree of the Year, and in 2015 it came fifth in Europe. Velke Opatovice has a railway station and the park is a short walk from the centre.
